text.p: Here are key facts about Guatemala, which on Sunday was due to sign a landmark agreement ending 36 years of guerrilla war.
AREA: 42,042 square miles (108,889 square km) bounded by Mexico to the north and west, the Pacific Ocean to the south and El Salvador, Honduras and Belize to the east.

POPULATION: 10 million, of which 60 percent are indigenous Maya. Eighty percent live in poverty and more than 50 percent are illiterate. Guatemala City, the capital, has about two million residents. Spanish is the official language, though 22 different Maya tongues are spoken. The country is predominantly Roman Catholic.

HISTORY: After gaining independence from Spain, which controlled it for nearly 300 years, Guatemala was ruled by a succession of strong dictators. A leftist government was ousted in a U.S.-backed coup in 1954, ending a 10-year experiment with democracy.

Three decades of nearly continuous military rule followed. A 1962 rebellion of army officers was the first manifestation of an insurgency that lasted 36 years. The army's counterinsurgency, backed by right-wing extremists, was marked by massacres, political assassinations and torture that gave Guatemala one of the worst human rights records in the world.
An estimated 140,000 Guatemalans, mostly civilians, were killed or forcibly "disappeared," during the war.

In the early 1980s four separate guerrilla fronts joined under the banner of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG). Under the military rule of Generals Romeo Lucas Garcia and Efrain Rios Montt, scorched-earth campaigns against suspected guerrilla support in the rural highlands triggered the flight of tens of thousands of Guatemalans -- some to refugee camps in Mexico, many to squatters settlements around the country.

Guatemala's recent history has been dominated by a gradual return to democracy -- four elected civilian presidents since 1986 -- and the weakening of military hold on political power. An arduous peace process began with direct negotiations between the government and the URNG in 1991, and has been brokered by the United Nations since 1994.

President Alvaro Arzu, a conservative businessman, was elected to a five-year term that began in January. Fighting came to an end in March as both sides ceased hostilities to further peace negotiations. Despite a crisis in the talks in October when a rebel faction kidnapped a rich Guatemalan woman, Arzu has fulfilled his promise to have a definitive peace treaty signed by the end of the year.

U.S.-GUATEMALAN RELATIONS: The country's traditionally warm relations with Washington soured in the 1970s when the Carter administration cut off military aid because of the country's abysmal human rights record. Relations have improved since the mid-1980s with the advance of democratic reforms in Guatemala. The United States has expressed strong confidence in Arzu and promised financial aid for post-war programmes in Guatemala.

ECONOMY: The country is heavily dependent on agriculture, and equitable distribution of land is a major problem, as is one of the lowest tax burden's in the Americas. Main exports include coffee, sugar, bananas and beef.
Guatemala has enjoyed growth rates in its Gross Domestic Product between 3.7 and 4.8 percent in the 1990s, with the growth rate projected to be 3 percent for 1996.
Guatemala currently has a $2 billion foreign debt.
